How was the weekend? Did you visit Aunt Teresa?
Yes! On Saturday we went to Toledo by train. We arrived at four.
First we visited the cathedral. Mihai took a hundred photos.
Then we walked along the city walls. The city is gorgeous.
And our aunt? Did she cook something special?
Yes, she made an amazing Castilian soup. And we ate marzipan, of course.
Mihai loved it. He bought two boxes for his family.
What time did you get back?

And you? What did you do?

Careful! HABLO (I speak, present) versus HABLÓ (he spoke, past). Only the accent tells them apart: HA-blo / ha-BLÓ.
The “yo” form is stressed on the last syllable: trabajÉ, comÍ, salÍ. Stress the last syllable clearly.
Llegué is read “ye-GEH” (hard g), and busqué “boos-KEH”: the u is silent and only keeps the sound.
This is the past tense for actions COMPLETED at a finished time: yesterday, last year, in 2015. It’s the basic storytelling tense, like the English simple past (“I ate”).
-ER and -IR verbs have the same endings. So you really only learn TWO sets of endings!
“Nosotros” is the same as in the present: hablamos = “we speak” and “we spoke”. The context (ayer, el año pasado) makes it clear.
2. Perfecto or indefinido? The clear rule
English chooses between “I have eaten” and “I ate” in a similar way. In Spain you choose by the time period:

Trick: if you can add “yesterday” or “last”, use the indefinido. If it’s “today” or “this”, use the perfecto (even where English would use the simple past: “This morning I had coffee” = “Esta mañana he tomado café”).
Don’t mix them: “Ayer he comido” is wrong in Spain, just like English “Yesterday I have eaten”. Correct: “Ayer comí”.
yesterday / last night / the day before yesterday
“Three years ago” = “HACE tres años”: HACE + time = ago, but it comes first.
To keep the same sound, some verbs change a letter in the “yo” form. The sound doesn’t change, only the spelling:
g + e would sound like “h”, so a u is added
c + e would sound like “th”, so it becomes qu
sacar (to take out, to take photos)
z doesn’t go before e, it becomes c
And verbs like leer: él leyó, ellos leyeron (i between vowels becomes y).
5. How to tell a story: connectors
A good story has an order. Use these words to link the actions:
Then we walked around the city.
Later we had dinner with our aunt.
In the end we went back to Madrid.
A few very common verbs (fui, hice, tuve, estuve…) are irregular. You saw them in the dialogue (hicisteis, vimos) and you’ll learn them in the next chapter.
Last Saturday I visited a museum.
What time did you (plural) get back?
Last night I watched a film.
Tom, Mihai’s English classmate, describes his first trip to Spain, ten years ago.
Ten years ago, in the summer of 2016, I travelled to Spain for the first time.
I arrived in Barcelona with my best friend, Jack. I didn’t speak any Spanish at all.
On the first day we visited the Sagrada Familia and walked along the Ramblas.
In the evening we looked for a restaurant. I ordered “chicken” and what came was… fish soup!
Jack laughed a lot. After that, I decided to learn Spanish.
The next day we took a train to Valencia. There we tried real paella.
We spent three days at the beach. We swam, sunbathed and ate a huge amount.
Then we travelled by bus to Granada and visited the Alhambra. I loved it!
There we met two girls from Seville, Rocío and Carmen.
They taught us our first Spanish words: “¡Olé!” and “¡Qué calor!” (How hot!).
In the end we went back to London very tanned and very happy.
Two years later I moved to Madrid. And here I still am!
next (“al día siguiente” = the next day)
¿Cuándo viajó Tom a España por primera vez?
Last Sunday, Lucía and her boyfriend Javier visited the Rastro, Madrid’s most famous market.
The Rastro has opened every Sunday for over four hundred years.
They arrived at ten in the morning. There were already lots of people in the streets.
First they wandered among the clothes stalls. Lucía bought a seventies skirt for only eight euros.
Then Javier found a stall with old records. He spent half an hour there and bought three jazz records.
Lucía got a little bored, so she wandered off to look at other things.
In a corner, an elderly lady was selling old objects: lamps, clocks, dolls and wooden boxes.
Lucía opened a small box and found a black-and-white photo inside.
In the photo was a young couple in front of a church. On the back, someone had written: “Rosario and Antonio, 1964”.
Lucía looked at the photo again. It was her grandmother! And her grandfather! It was their wedding photo.
The lady explained that she had bought the box many years ago from a house in the neighbourhood.
Lucía paid two euros for the box and ran back to Javier.
That afternoon they visited Grandma Rosario and gave her the box.
Grandma looked at the photo in silence for a minute. Then she cried and laughed at the same time.
“I lost this photo in a house move forty years ago,” she said. “Thank you, my dear. It’s the most beautiful present of my life.”
Since that Sunday, the photo has stood in the living room, next to the wall clock. Grandma looks at it every morning as she drinks her coffee.
